title: AI Sales Assistant Without a Meeting Bot
summary: What an AI sales assistant without a meeting bot is, how botless capture works, and the honest trade-offs against bot-based recorders like Fathom and Otter.
body_markdown:
You have probably watched it happen: the call connects, and before anyone says hello, "Notetaker has joined the meeting" appears in the participant list. An AI sales assistant without a meeting bot avoids that moment by capturing audio locally on the rep's computer, so no extra participant ever joins the call.


## 01


What is an AI sales assistant without a meeting bot?


It is a sales tool that listens to the call through the rep's own machine instead of joining the meeting as a virtual attendee. A small desktop app captures the audio the rep already hears and speaks, transcribes it, and feeds it to the assistant. The participant list shows only the people who are actually in the meeting.


Contrast that with the default mode of most recorders, including Fathom, Otter, and Avoma: a bot joins the meeting as a named participant, records from inside it, and everyone can see it there.


Both routes end in a transcript. The difference is what the prospect experiences on the way.


## 02


Why the visible bot changes the meeting


A bot in the participant list is not neutral. Three things happen often enough that sales teams should plan for them.


**Prospects ask about it.** "What's Notetaker?" is now a common first question on discovery calls. The rep spends the opening minute explaining a recording tool instead of building rapport. It is a small cost, but it lands at the worst possible moment: the start of a first conversation.


**Legal and security teams block it.** A bot is an external service joining a confidential conversation, and some organisations treat it that way. Conferencing admins can hold unknown participants in the waiting room or reject them by policy. When that happens, the recorder gets nothing, usually on exactly the calls that matter most: large accounts with strict IT.


**It announces recording before trust exists.** Disclosure is right, and often legally required. But a bot forces the disclosure into the first ten seconds, framed by a third-party product name the prospect has never agreed to. A rep who discloses in their own words, at a moment of their choosing, keeps control of that conversation.


None of this makes bots wrong. It makes them a trade-off, and a trade-off should be chosen deliberately, with the costs in view.


## 03


Bot-based vs botless: the honest comparison


Bot-based capture Botless (local) capture


How it works A virtual participant joins the call and records from inside A desktop app captures audio on the rep's machine


Visible to prospects Yes, as a named participant No extra participant appears


Deployment Easy: connect a calendar, the bot joins every meeting Needs a desktop app installed on each rep's computer


Platform coverage Broad: works with any platform the bot can join (Zoom, Meet, Teams) Depends on the app; capture happens below the meeting platform, but OS support matters (many tools are Mac-first)


Can be blocked Yes, by waiting rooms or admin policy No, nothing external joins the call


Consent obligations Same law applies Same law applies


Works when the rep is not host Bot may need admission by the host Yes, capture is on the rep's side


Fit for real-time assistance Possible, but the bot's presence shapes the call it is helping with Strong: audio is already local and low-latency, help shows only to the rep


Two honest points from that table.


First, bots earned their popularity. An admin connects the team's calendars once and every meeting is covered, on any platform, on any device, with nothing installed. For a RevOps leader rolling out call recording to two hundred reps, that is a real advantage. Botless capture requires a desktop app on each machine, and most botless tools support macOS and Windows but not calls taken purely on a phone or tablet.


Second, and this matters: **botless does not remove consent obligations.** The law regulates recording, not participant lists. Some jurisdictions require one party's consent, others require everyone's, and calls often cross borders. Removing the bot removes the awkward announcement, but the disclosure duty stays with the rep and the company. "Invisible" describes the participant list; your legal position is a separate question. This is not legal advice; check the rules where you and your prospects sit.


## 04


Why real-time assistance favours botless capture


A meeting recorder can afford to be visible, because its work happens after the call. A real-time assistant cannot wait: it listens live and surfaces answers while the prospect is still talking, which is the whole point of[a real-time sales assistant](https://www.caretta.so/blog/what-is-a-real-time-sales-assistant) .


That changes the architecture question. Real-time help needs live audio either way, and local capture fits it naturally: the audio is already on the rep's machine with no round trip through a bot, and the output (a suggested answer, a pricing fact, a competitor rebuttal) appears only on the rep's screen. The prospect sees a normal call. The rep sees help.


This is the design Caretta uses. It captures the call locally through a desktop app, no bot joins, and answers drawn from your docs, CRM, and past calls appear beside the meeting window as the conversation happens. You can see how the pieces fit on the[product page](https://www.caretta.so/product) .


## 05


Which should you choose?


Choose bot-based capture if you mainly need recordings and summaries after the call, you want zero-install rollout across a large team, and your prospects rarely push back on a visible notetaker.


Choose botless capture if a visible bot is costing you meetings or opening minutes, your buyers' security teams block external participants, or you want live in-call assistance rather than a post-call summary. If live assistance is the goal, compare the current options in[our rundown of real-time AI sales assistants](https://www.caretta.so/blog/best-real-time-ai-sales-assistants) .


Either way, write down your disclosure practice before you roll anything out. The capture method is an engineering choice. Consent is not.
